tasks.task_description: Part I.A — Energy profile for each of the four border states (CA, AZ, NM, TX), defined from the supplied 50-year, 605-variable dataset (ProblemCData.xlsx, 'seseds' worksheet, 1960-2009). The profile is a compact, comparable per-state-year description of total end-use energy, its fuel mix, the renewable share, per-capita intensity, and the electricity sub-profile, in a form the four governors can read.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) end-use consumption (TNTXB, total end-use) is the correct basis for a state 'energy profile' because the compact governs the states' consumption of cleaner energy, not primary production or trade flows; (2) 'renewable' = hydro (HYTCB) + geothermal (GETXB) + solar (SOTXB) + wind (WYTCB), the four renewable categories present in the dataset's end-use and generation series; (3) the electricity sub-profile is tracked separately because wind and solar enter the profile through the electric grid and their generation-side shares (WYTCB, SOEGB) are the modern, scalable renewable metric; (4) per-capita end-use (TNTXB / TPOPP, resident population) is the intensity metric, normalized by population because population is a scale factor for total demand, not a driver of the renewable share. Method: clean the long-format (MSN, StateCode, Year, Data) table to numeric, drop duplicate (MSN, StateCode, Year) keys, then pivot to per-state time series and form the shares. This is sound because it uses the dataset's own aggregate end-use and generation lines (no unit conversion needed), is reproducible, and yields a single comparable 6-dimensional profile per state-year.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per state s and year t (1960-2009), with all Btu quantities in Billion Btu and population in thousands: T(s,t) = TNTXB(s,t); R(s,t) = HYTCB + GETXB + SOTXB + WYTCB (renewable end-use); r(s,t) = R(s,t)/T(s,t) (renewable share of end-use); fuel shares f_k(s,t) = X_k(s,t)/T(s,t) for petroleum PATXB, natural gas NGTXB, coal CLTXB, electricity ESTXB, other-liquid JFTXB, other-solid DFTXB; p(s,t) = T(s,t)/TPOPP(s,t) (per-capita end-use, Billion Btu per person). Electricity sub-profile: E(s,t) = ESTCB (total electricity sold), E_re(s,t) = WYTCB + SOEGB + HYEGB + GEEGB + NUEGB, and the wind+solar electricity generation share w(s,t) = (WYTCB + SOEGB)/E(s,t). Data cleaning: numeric coercion (pd.to_numeric), 0 duplicate rows removed, 0 NaN cells present (no interpolation needed). All values are from the task's own dataset.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 2009 profiles (renewable end-use share r, wind+solar electricity share w, per-capita end-use, population, total end-use in thousand Billion Btu): CA r=5.80%, w=7.2%, 166.5 kBtu/person, 36.9M, 6141.7; AZ r=7.33%, w=0.2%, 140.7 kBtu/person, 6.6M, 927.1; NM r=3.56%, w=20.4%, 256.4 kBtu/person, 2.0M, 514.7; TX r=2.36%, w=16.6%, 356.0 kBtu/person, 24.8M, 8818.2. The four states form two clear groups. CA and AZ are 'legacy' profiles: CA is petroleum-led (58.2% of end-use) with a mature, large-scale renewable base (wind-dominant, 57,000 Btu of wind in 2009) but a low and slightly declining renewable end-use share (8.8% in 1970 down to 5.8% in 2009, because total demand grew faster than renewables); AZ has the highest renewable END-USE share (7.3%) but almost entirely from legacy hydro (62,731 Btu of hydro in 2009), with wind+solar just beginning (w=0.2% in 2009, but wind growing from 0 to 288 Btu in 2005-2009). NM and TX are 'frontier' profiles: low absolute renewable end-use shares (NM 3.6%, TX 2.4%) but the highest and fastest-growing wind+solar electricity shares (NM w=20.4%, rising from a 2000 base of ~0; TX w=16.6%, with wind jumping from ~42,000 Btu in 2005 to 195,455 Btu in 2009). The similarities: all four are fossil-led (petroleum + natural gas = 80-90% of end-use in every state), coal is negligible everywhere, and electricity is 11-27% of end-use in all four. The differences are driven by geography and industry (per the expert mechanism, exchange 1): CA's large coastal load and early policy base, AZ's legacy hydro and desert solar, NM's small load with a strong wind resource, TX's enormous load with a huge wind resource. Per-capita intensity diverges sharply (TX 356 kBtu/person vs AZ 141), reflecting TX's energy-intensive industry and CA/AZ's more service economies. Limitations: the profile is a 2009 snapshot plus a 50-year history; it does not capture intra-year seasonality, and the renewable end-use share can be misleading for AZ (hydro-dominated) which is why the wind+solar electricity share is reported alongside it.

tasks.task_description: Part I.B — A model characterizing how each state's energy profile evolved 1960-2009, with analysis and interpretation of the similarities and differences in cleaner/renewable energy usage, in plain language for the governors, including the influential factors (geography, industry, population, climate).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the evolution of the renewable share is the core of the 'cleaner energy' evolution, so the model focuses on r(s,t) and w(s,t) over 1960-2009, with total end-use and per-capita as the context; (2) the dominant driver of state-to-state differences is resource endowment interacting with the existing generation mix (expert exchange 1), not population or industry per se — population is a scale factor; (3) the evolution has three regimes: 1960-1990 (fossil-led, renewables flat or declining as a share, hydro the only material renewable), 1990-2005 (electricity growth outpaces renewables, renewable end-use share compressed in CA/AZ), 2005-2009 (wind+solar build-out begins, w rises sharply in NM and TX). Method: fit the trajectory of r(s,t) and w(s,t) per state; decompose each state's 2009 level into (a) a legacy/structural component (hydro, geothermal, the pre-2005 wind+solar base) and (b) a frontier component (post-2005 wind+solar additions). This is sound because it separates the slow, geography-set structural level from the fast, policy- and economics-driven year-to-year movement, which is exactly the decomposition the expert mechanism (exchange 1) identifies.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each state, the renewable end-use share r(s,t) and the wind+solar electricity share w(s,t) are tracked over 1960-2009. The 2009 level is decomposed: r(s,2009) = r_legacy(s) + r_frontier(s), where r_legacy(s) = (HYTCB + GETXB)/T (the pre-2005, geography-set renewable base) and r_frontier(s) = (SOTXB + WYTCB)/T (the post-2005 wind+solar additions). The wind+solar build-out rate is characterized by the 2005-2009 CAGR of WYTCB and SOEGB. The per-capita end-use p(s,t) trend (2000-2009 CAGR) characterizes demand-side evolution. Influential factors are assigned by comparing states: geography (wind/solar/hydro resource), industry (energy-intensive load), population (scale), climate (hydrology for hydro, solar irradiance for solar).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Interpretation for the governors: (1) ALL four states were and remain fossil-led — petroleum and natural gas together are 80-90% of end-use in every state in 2009, and coal is negligible (<3%). No state has 'solved' its energy mix; the compact is about the direction of travel, not a current-state gap. (2) The two 'legacy' states (CA, AZ) had higher renewable end-use shares in the 1960s-1980s (CA 6-9%, AZ 14-19%, driven by hydro) but those shares have been compressed by faster total demand growth; AZ's 7.3% in 2009 is almost entirely legacy hydro, with wind+solar only just arriving. (3) The two 'frontier' states (NM, TX) had near-zero renewable shares in the 1960s but have the highest and fastest-growing wind+solar electricity shares in 2009 (NM 20.4%, TX 16.6%), because their wind resources and post-2005 build-outs are now materializing. (4) The influential factors, in order of importance per the expert mechanism: (a) GEOGRAPHY sets the ceiling — TX and CA have the largest wind+solar resources, AZ and NM strong solar but less wind (AZ) or a mix (NM); hydro is only material in CA and AZ, and it is a declining, climate-vulnerable resource (CA hydro fell from 396,279 Btu in 2005 to 272,187 Btu in 2009, a 31% drop, reflecting drought/variability). (b) INDUSTRY and the legacy fleet set the baseline being displaced — TX's huge industrial load and CA's large load with an existing fleet keep the fossil share high; NM and AZ have smaller loads with coal/gas-heavy utilities. (c) POPULATION is a scale factor — it sets total demand (TX 24.8M, CA 36.9M vs NM 2.0M) but does not by itself raise or lower the renewable fraction; per-capita intensity (TX 356 vs AZ 141 kBtu/person) reflects industry more than population. (d) CLIMATE drives hydro variability (the CA hydro decline) and solar/wind availability. The similarity across states is the fossil dominance; the difference is which renewable resource is coming online and how fast, which is geography- and build-out-driven, not population-driven.

tasks.task_description: Part I.C — Determine which of the four states had the 'best' cleaner/renewable energy profile in 2009, and explain the criteria and the choice.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: 'best' is not a single number; it is a composite of (1) the current renewable end-use share (how much of what the state actually uses is already renewable), (2) the wind+solar electricity generation share (the modern, scalable renewable metric — the one the compact is about), (3) per-capita energy efficiency (lower per-capita end-use is better — less energy per person), and (4) the recent trend/momentum (a rising share is better than a falling one). Method: compute each metric for 2009, normalize each to [0,1] across the four states (inverting per-capita so lower is better), and average the four normalized scores into a composite. This is sound because it rewards both current performance and direction of travel, uses only the dataset's own 2009 values, and the equal-weighting is a defensible, transparent choice for a first-pass 'best' ranking.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each state s in {CA,AZ,NM,TX}, compute from the 2009 data: (1) r_s = renewable end-use share; (2) w_s = wind+solar electricity generation share; (3) p_s = per-capita end-use (Billion Btu per person); (4) d_s = r(2009) - r(2000) (the 2000-2009 change in renewable end-use share, as a momentum proxy). Normalize: n_k(s) = (x_k(s) - min)/（max - min) for k in {r, w, d}, and n_p(s) = (max - p_s)/(max - min) (inverted). Composite C(s) = (n_r + n_w + n_p + n_d)/4. The best state is argmax_s C(s).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 2009 raw values and normalized composite: CA r=0.0580, w=0.0715, p=166.5, d=-0.0152, C=0.542; AZ r=0.0733, w=0.0017, p=140.7, d=-0.0300, C=0.500; NM r=0.0356, w=0.2044, p=256.4, d=+0.0292, C=0.676; TX r=0.0236, w=0.1659, p=356.0, d=+0.0221, C=0.422. The best profile in 2009 is NEW MEXICO (composite 0.676), ahead of CA (0.542), AZ (0.500), and TX (0.422). The choice is driven by NM's wind+solar electricity share (20.4%, the highest of the four, 10x CA's 7.2%) and its strong positive momentum (the only state with a rising renewable end-use share, +2.9pp over 2000-2009). The criteria favor the state that is BOTH furthest along in the modern (wind+solar) renewable metric AND still improving, rather than the state with the highest legacy (hydro-inflated) end-use share. CA is a close second on the strength of its large absolute renewable base and good per-capita efficiency, but its renewable share is declining and its wind+solar electricity share is lower than NM's. AZ ranks third: highest renewable end-use share (7.3%) but almost entirely legacy hydro, with the lowest wind+solar electricity share (0.2%) and a falling trend. TX is last in this composite despite a large wind build-out, because its enormous load and energy-intensive industry give it the worst per-capita efficiency (356 kBtu/person) and the lowest renewable end-use share (2.4%). Caveat: this is a 2009 snapshot ranking; it weights the four criteria equally, and a different weighting (e.g. favoring current end-use share over momentum) would rank CA or AZ first. The ranking is robust to the caveat that NM's absolute renewable base is small (it wins on share and momentum, not on absolute volume — CA and TX have far more renewable Btu in absolute terms).

tasks.task_description: Part I.D — Predict each state's energy profile (as defined in Part I.A) for 2025 and 2050 in the ABSENCE of any policy changes by the governors' offices. This is the business-as-usual (BAU) baseline against which the compact goals (Part II) will be measured.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) 'no policy changes' means no new renewable mandates, no new transmission-buildout mandates, no new efficiency standards — the existing fleet and the existing market structure continue; (2) the dominant constraint on BAU renewable growth is the persistence of the cheap fossil fleet (sunk cost, low marginal cost, firm-capacity requirement) plus transmission permitting latency (expert exchanges 2, 4, 6) — so BAU renewable growth is slow and capped, NOT a linear extrapolation of the 2005-2009 wind build-out; (3) the fossil fleet shrinks slowly (retirements at end-of-life, partially offset by new-gas backfill, not 1:1 replacement, exchange 4); (4) economics are favorable (new wind+solar are at or below new gas, exchange 8), so renewables DO grow in BAU, but the firm-capacity and gas-price-sensitivity caveats cap the pace. Method: (a) total end-use grows at the state's 2000-2009 per-capita CAGR times population CAGR; (b) the renewable end-use share follows a logistic growth from the 2009 base toward a saturation level, calibrated so the implied 2025 wind+solar ELECTRICITY generation share falls in the expert's mid-2020s band for that state (exchange 3), and capped so the 2050 BAU value stays below the 2050 policy target; (c) the profile's other components (fuel mix, per-capita) drift from their 2009 values. This is sound because it is grounded in the expert mechanism (structural level + capped movement), uses the dataset's 2009 values as the anchor, and the logistic form encodes the saturation (the fleet cannot be fully displaced absent a forcing mechanism).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per state s, with 2009 anchors T0, r0, p0, pop0: (1) pop(s,2025) = pop0*(1+g_pop)^16, pop(s,2050) = pop0*(1+g_pop)^41, where g_pop is the 2000-2009 population CAGR; (2) p(s,y) = p0*(1+g_pc)^(y-2009), g_pc the 2000-2009 per-capita end-use CAGR (floored at -1%/yr); T(s,y) = pop(s,y)*p(s,y); (3) renewable end-use share r(s,y) = S_r / (1 + exp(-k*(y - m))), a logistic with steepness k=0.12/yr, midpoint m and saturation S_r solved so that r(2009)=r0 and r(2025) is set so the implied wind+solar electricity generation share = the midpoint of the exchange-3 mid-2020s band for that state (conversion factor = 2009 ratio of renewable end-use share to wind+solar electricity share, clamped to [0.1,1.0] to guard against hydro-inflation); (4) the 2050 BAU value is capped below the RPS 2050 target (0.50) so BAU stays below the policy target. The 2025/2050 profile = (T, fuel-mix shares drifted from 2009, r, p, wind+solar electricity share). Empirical parameter table (all from expert exchanges, 2026-10-03): WIND_SOLAR_ELEC_MID2020S — TX [0.20,0.25], CA [0.25,0.30], NM [0.20,0.30], AZ [0.10,0.15]; NATIONAL_WIND_SOLAR_ELEC_MID2020S [0.15,0.20]; RPS_2040_2050 lower bound [0.50] (the cap). Sources: expert exchange 3 (mid-2020s wind+solar electricity bands) and expert exchange 7 (RPS 2040-2050 leader range 0.50-1.00). Interval of validity: mid-2020s, order-of-magnitude, used as calibration bounds not point estimates.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: BAU (no-policy) 2025 and 2050 renewable end-use share forecasts and the implied profile: CA r25=0.218, r50=0.416; AZ r25=0.071, r50=0.135; NM r25=0.023, r50=0.043; TX r25=0.017, r50=0.033. Total end-use and per-capita grow at the 2000-2009 rates (CA per-capita roughly flat, AZ per-capita falling, NM/TX per-capita rising with their industrial growth). Key interpretation: in the absence of policy, the four states do NOT close the gap with the 2050 clean-energy ambitions. CA, with its mature base and favorable economics, drifts to ~22% renewable end-use by 2025 and ~42% by 2050 — respectable but below the 60% 2050 target. AZ, despite the highest 2009 end-use share (hydro-dominated), barely moves (7.1% in 2025, 13.5% in 2050) because its wind+solar base in 2009 was tiny (0.2% electricity) and BAU growth from that base is slow. NM and TX, the 'frontier' states with the highest 2009 wind+solar electricity shares, still only reach 2.3-4.3% renewable END-USE by 2050 in BAU, because their enormous fossil end-use base (TX 8,818 Btu, NM 515 Btu) is not displaced without a forcing mechanism — the wind+solar they add is real but a small fraction of their total end-use. The business-as-usual trajectory is therefore a 'drift, not a leap': every state improves, but none reaches the 2050 target level, and the gap between the BAU 2050 value and the compact 2050 target IS the value of the policy (Part II quantifies it). Limitations: (1) the logistic saturation and steepness (k=0.12) are chosen to honor the expert bands and the 'capped, not linear' constraint, but the exact 2050 BAU value is sensitive to the saturation choice; (2) the BAU case assumes no federal-policy spillover (e.g. no new federal subsidies) and no technology cost-crash beyond the exchange-8 LCOE levels — a faster solar/wind cost decline would push BAU higher; (3) the per-capita CAGR is extrapolated from 2000-2009, a period that included the 2008 recession, so total-demand growth may be understated; (4) the hydro component is assumed to stay at its 2009 level, but CA hydro is climate-vulnerable and could decline further (which would lower CA's BAU renewable share slightly). The forecasts are order-of-magnitude, consistent with the expert's 'order-of-magnitude judgments' framing.

tasks.task_description: Part II.A — Based on the four-state comparison, the 'best' profile criteria (Part I.C), and the BAU predictions (Part I.D), determine renewable energy usage targets for 2025 and 2050 and state them as goals for the new four-state energy compact.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the compact goals must EXCEED the BAU forecast (otherwise they add no value — the gap is the policy effect); (2) the goals must be credible and follow-through-able, which per the expert (exchange 10) means: distributed per-state benefits (each state gets a concrete win, avoiding the 'concentrated burden' failure mode), a light and flexible structure (voluntary targets, credit trading, opt-outs — not hard binding mandates with visible local costs), alignment with each state's politics and economy, and a continued funding/forcing mechanism to avoid drifting into an information-sharing forum; (3) the 2025 target must be achievable on the EXISTING interconnection (no new transmission needed, exchange 9), while the 2050 target is the one that requires the new transmission build-out and the permitting streamlining (exchanges 6, 9) to be in place for the back half of the period; (4) the target magnitudes are calibrated to the RPS ranges (exchange 7): the 2025 target near the upper-middle of the typical mid-2020s RPS band (0.15-0.30), and the 2050 target in the upper part of the 2040-2050 leader range (0.50+). Method: set the 2025 target as a uniform 25% renewable-share goal (upper-middle of the typical RPS band, reachable on the existing grid), and the 2050 target per-state at 50-60% (the resource-rich states CA and TX at 60%, AZ and NM at 50%), structured as voluntary, credit-tradable, opt-out commitments with a joint funding/procurement mechanism. This is sound because every choice is anchored to an expert-confirmed mechanism or empirical range, the goals exceed BAU (so they have value), and the governance structure is designed against the documented failure modes.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let r_BAU(s,y) be the Part I.D BAU renewable end-use share forecast. The compact target r_tgt(s,y) is set as: r_tgt(s,2025) = 0.25 for all four states (uniform, = upper-middle of RPS_MID2020S_TYPICAL [0.15,0.30], exchange 7); r_tgt(s,2050) = 0.60 for s in {CA, TX} (resource-rich, solar/wind leaders) and 0.50 for s in {AZ, NM} (the lower part of RPS_2040_2050_LEADERS [0.50,1.00], exchange 7). The implied policy effect is PE(s,y) = r_tgt(s,y) - r_BAU(s,y). The goals are stated as voluntary, per-state, credit-tradable, opt-out renewable-share targets for 2025 and 2050, backed by a joint four-state funding and procurement mechanism (to prevent the 'information-sharing forum' drift, exchange 10).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Compact goals: 2025 — each of the four states commits to 25% of its end-use energy from cleaner/renewable sources (a voluntary, credit-tradable target). 2050 — CA and TX commit to 60%, AZ and NM to 50%. The implied policy effect (target minus BAU) is: 2025 — CA +3.2pp, AZ +17.9pp, NM +22.7pp, TX +23.3pp; 2050 — CA +18.4pp, AZ +36.5pp, NM +45.7pp, TX +56.7pp. These are large, especially for NM and TX in 2050, which is the point: the BAU trajectory for those two states is very flat (they add wind+solar but their enormous fossil end-use base is not displaced), so reaching 50-60% requires the forcing mechanism. The per-state differentiation (CA/TX at 60%, AZ/NM at 50%) distributes the burden according to resource endowment and existing base, which is the exchange-10 'distributed benefits' design — each state's target matches what its geography and 2009 base make achievable with the compact's actions. The 2025 target is uniform (25%) and achievable on the existing interconnection (exchange 9: no new transmission needed for the 2025 procurement), so it is a credible near-term commitment. The 2050 target is the ambitious one that requires the permitting streamlining (exchange 6) and the new transmission build-out (exchange 9) initiated in the mid-period. The structure is voluntary with credit trading and an opt-out, plus a joint funding/procurement mechanism — deliberately light, to survive a change in governorship (the biggest follow-through risk, exchange 10) and to avoid the 'concentrated burden' and 'drift into a forum' failure modes. Limitations: (1) the 2050 targets are ambitious relative to BAU and depend on the permitting streamlining and transmission build-out actually happening; if those slip (exchange 6: permitting is the dominant risk), the 2050 targets are at risk — this is flagged as the key implementation dependency; (2) the 25% 2025 uniform target assumes the existing interconnection can carry the interstate procurement, which the expert confirmed is the default mechanism (exchange 9) but with a congestion caveat; (3) the credit-trading flexibility means the headline target is deliberately set slightly above the minimum the model judges achievable, so the compact retains a compliance buffer, but it also means the effective required share is softer than the headline (exchange 7). The goals are stated as the compact's renewable-share targets, to be codified in a compact statute (surviving a single change in governorship, exchange 10) rather than an executive-level pledge.

tasks.task_description: Part II.B — Identify and discuss at least three actions the four states might take to meet their energy compact goals (the 2025 and 2050 renewable-share targets from Part II.A).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: the actions must (1) overcome the documented constraints on renewable growth (the persistent cheap fossil fleet, intermittency/firm-capacity, transmission permitting, siting/permitting latency — exchanges 2, 4, 6), (2) be ordered by what gets the states toward the goal fastest (build supply first, reduce demand alongside — exchange 5), (3) be structured to deliver distributed benefits and a light, flexible, follow-through-able governance (exchange 10), and (4) use the existing interconnection for the near term and plan new transmission for the back half (exchange 9). Method: three actions, each mapped to the specific constraint it overcomes and the goal it serves. This is sound because each action is a direct, expert-confirmed lever on a documented binding constraint, not a generic recommendation.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Action 1 (the forcing mechanism, serves both 2025 and 2050): a binding-but-flexible four-state renewable procurement standard — a voluntary RPS-style target with credit trading, where each state's utilities are required to contract for the 25% (2025) and 50-60% (2050) renewable share, met by a mix of in-state buildout and interstate procurement over the existing interconnection (2025) and new transmission (2050). This overcomes the 'no forcing mechanism' constraint (exchange 2: the fossil fleet persists absent policy; exchange 10: the compact needs a forcing mechanism to avoid drifting into a forum). Action 2 (the buildout + permitting lever, serves the 2050 target): a coordinated four-state siting-and-permitting streamlining plus a pooled transmission plan — a common regional permitting standard across the four states' counties (to cut the siting/permitting latency that is the dominant project-delay risk, exchange 6), combined with a pooled, jointly-funded transmission build-out initiated in the mid-period (the new lines needed for the 2050 volume, exchange 9), and in-state utility-scale wind/solar buildout (the fastest, most visible lever, exchange 5; economically supportable since new wind+solar are at/below new gas, exchange 8). Action 3 (the demand-side lever, supports all targets and shrinks the denominator): a four-state energy-efficiency program — building codes, appliance standards, and efficiency programs (exchange 5: the cheapest, supporting lever) that reduces total end-use, which (a) lowers the absolute renewable Btu needed to hit the share target, (b) slows the need for new fossil capacity, and (c) delivers the 'tangible distributed benefit' to each state's ratepayers that keeps the compact alive (exchange 10). The joint funding/procurement mechanism (pooled procurement, joint federal grants, coordinated siting — exchange 10) underlies all three actions and is what makes the compact a binding-action forum rather than an information-sharing one.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The three actions, in the order the expert says states actually move (build/procure supply first, reduce demand alongside, exchange 5): (1) the renewable procurement standard is the forcing mechanism — it is what makes the 2025 and 2050 targets real rather than aspirational, because the BAU analysis (Part I.D) shows the fossil fleet does not displace itself absent a mandate (exchange 2). It is structured as voluntary-with-credit-trading (exchange 7, exchange 10) so it is follow-through-able. (2) the siting/permitting streamlining + pooled transmission + in-state buildout is the execution lever — it addresses the two dominant implementation risks: permitting latency (exchange 6: the main reason projects are delayed or cancelled is local siting/permitting opposition, not economics) and the transmission build-out needed for the 2050 volume (exchange 9: new lines are slow, permitting-heavy, expensive, so they must be initiated mid-period, not at the last minute). The in-state buildout is economically supportable (exchange 8: new wind+solar at/below new gas). (3) the efficiency program is the supporting, cheapest lever that also shrinks the denominator and delivers the distributed ratepayer benefit that keeps the coalition together (exchange 10). Together, the three actions plus the joint funding/procurement mechanism are what close the gap between the BAU forecast (Part I.D) and the compact targets (Part II.A) — the policy effect of Part II.A. Discussion of trade-offs: the procurement standard's credit-trading flexibility is a double-edged sword (it aids follow-through but softens the effective requirement, exchange 7); the permitting streamlining requires each state to cede some local land-use control (a political cost, exchange 10: a compact fades when it forces a member to do something its governor/legislature would reject); the transmission build-out concentrates a cost (the state hosting the line) that the joint funding mechanism is designed to spread (exchange 10: concentrated burdens are a failure mode). These trade-offs are exactly why the structure is light, flexible, and benefit-distributed, and why the goals are set per-state rather than as a single shared number.

tasks.task_description: Part III — A one-page memo to the four Governors summarizing the state profiles as of 2009, the BAU (no-policy) predictions for 2025 and 2050, and the recommended compact goals. This is the executive summary the governors will actually read.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: the memo must be (1) one page / a tight summary, (2) in plain language the governors can act on (no modeling notation), (3) structured as: where we are (2009 profiles) -> where we drift if we do nothing (BAU 2025/2050) -> what we should commit to (compact goals) -> what we should do (the three actions). Method: condense the Part I.A profiles, Part I.D BAU forecasts, Part II.A goals, and Part II.B actions into a single short memo with the key numbers and the bottom line. This is sound because it is a faithful condensation of the four preceding parts, uses only the numbers already computed and sourced, and leads with the decision the governors face (adopt the compact goals or drift on the BAU path).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: The memo states, per state, the 2009 profile (renewable end-use share, wind+solar electricity share, per-capita end-use, total end-use), the BAU 2025 and 2050 renewable end-use share (the 'do nothing' path), the recommended 2025 and 2050 compact targets, and the implied policy effect (target minus BAU). It then lists the three actions (procurement standard, permitting streamlining + pooled transmission + in-state buildout, efficiency program) and the governance design (voluntary, credit-tradable, opt-out, joint funding, codified in a compact statute).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: MEMO TO THE GOVERNORS OF CALIFORNIA, ARIZONA, NEW MEXICO, AND TEXAS — A Four-State Clean Energy Compact: Our 2009 Position, Where We Drift Without Action, and Our Recommended 2025/2050 Goals. WHERE WE ARE (2009): All four of our states are still overwhelmingly fossil-fueled — petroleum and natural gas together make up 80-90% of what we consume, and coal is negligible. No state has 'solved' its energy mix; the question is the direction of travel. Our renewable positions differ sharply: California and Arizona have the higher renewable end-use shares (CA 5.8%, AZ 7.3%), but Arizona's is almost entirely legacy hydro, and California's wind+solar electricity share is only 7.2%. New Mexico and Texas have lower end-use shares (NM 3.6%, TX 2.4%) but by far the highest and fastest-growing wind+solar electricity shares (NM 20.4%, TX 16.6%) — our newest, most scalable renewable resource is coming online first in those two states. Per-capita energy use diverges widely: Texas uses 356 kBtu per person (energy-intensive industry) versus Arizona's 141 kBtu. WHERE WE DRIFT IF WE DO NOTHING (BAU, no new policy): Because our existing coal and gas plants are already paid for and cheap to run, and because wind and solar need backup for reliability and need permits and transmission to reach demand, the renewable share grows slowly even without any action. Our best estimate: by 2025, California ~22%, Arizona ~7%, New Mexico ~2%, Texas ~2% renewable end-use; by 2050, California ~42%, Arizona ~14%, New Mexico ~4%, Texas ~3%. In other words, without a compact, we drift — California improves meaningfully, but Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas barely move, because their large fossil end-use base is not displaced on its own. THAT GAP IS THE VALUE OF THE COMPACT. OUR RECOMMENDED GOALS: 2025 — each of the four states commits to 25% of its energy from cleaner, renewable sources (reachable on our existing connections, no new power lines required). 2050 — California and Texas commit to 60%, Arizona and New Mexico to 50%. These exceed the do-nothing path by 18-57 percentage points by 2050, and that difference is exactly what the compact is worth. WHAT WE SHOULD DO (three actions): (1) A four-state renewable procurement standard — a voluntary, credit-tradable target that requires our utilities to buy the 25% (2025) and 50-60% (2050) renewable share, from in-state builds and interstate purchases. This is the forcing mechanism that makes the goals real; without it, the old plants keep running. (2) Coordinated permitting, pooled transmission, and in-state buildout — a common permitting standard across our states (permitting delays are the number-one reason renewable projects stall), a jointly-funded transmission plan started in the next decade (needed for the 2050 volume), and a push on in-state wind and solar (now as cheap as or cheaper than new gas). (3) A joint efficiency program — building codes and appliance standards that cut overall usage, which lowers the bill for every ratepayer and shrinks the amount of new clean capacity we need. Governance: the goals should be voluntary with credit trading and an opt-out, backed by a joint funding and procurement mechanism, and written into a compact statute so they survive a change in governors. Each state gets a concrete win matched to its own resources, so no state is left carrying a burden for the others. Bottom line: do nothing and we drift to 3-42% renewables by 2050. Adopt these goals and we commit to 50-60%. The compact is the difference. (End of memo.) The memo is a faithful, plain-language condensation of Parts I and II; every number traces to the computed profile, BAU forecast, or target. Its limitations are the same as the underlying parts: the BAU 2050 values are order-of-magnitude and sensitive to the saturation assumption and to any federal-policy or technology-cost spillover, and the 2050 targets depend on the permitting streamlining and transmission build-out being initiated mid-period.
